questions.problem:
Given the following piecewise function $f(x),$ what is $f(5)?$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}4,\, & x\le 5 \\ 5,\, & x>5\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x=5$ is in the interval $x\le 5,$ we use the left-hand branch, namely $f(x)=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(5) & =4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given the following piecewise function $f(x),$ what is $f(1)?$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2x+7,\, & x\le 1 \\ 2x-3,\, & x>1\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x=1$ is in the interval $x\le 1,$ we use the left-hand branch, namely $f(x)=2x+7:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =2(1)+7 \\  & =2+7 \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We will graph each branch separately.

- On the interval $(-\infty ,3],$ we have a line with a slope of $\frac{1}{3}$ and $y$-intercept $0.$ So the graph is the line $y=\frac{1}{3}x$ that ends at $(3,1),$ including this point.

- On the interval $(3,\infty ),$ we have a horizontal line that passes through the point $(3,2).$ So the graph is the line $y=2$ that starts at $(3,2),$ excluding this point.

Therefore, the function is defined as follows:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}x,\, & x\le 3 \\ 2,\, & x>3.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
For the function $g(x)$ defined on the set of integers, find $g(-12)$ and $g(3),$ where $g(x)$ is the following piecewise function:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192535/assets/43ec07dcf63fdaf3f85bd576c64da4f4afccee23143cfe51c337dd3e3e855cce.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
- First, we compute $g(-12).$ Since $-12 < 1,$ we use the first branch:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =2x \\ g(-12) & =2(-12) \\  & =-24\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we compute $g(3).$ Since $3 \geq 1,$ we use the second branch:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =3x \\ g(3) & =3(3) \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    The Domain of a Piecewise Function
canonical_examples.problem:
What is the domain of the function shown below?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14192535/assets/2b0235b4a984b1560312cef1c315ca8955bf062a90b75c3e03df8ee027e3cbd4.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function is defined for values between $-4$ and $1.$

- Since there is an open circle at $x=-4,$ this point is not included in the domain.

- Since there is a closed circle at $x=-1,$ this point is included in the domain.

- Since there is an open circle at $x=1,$ this point is not included in the domain.

So, the function $f(x)$ above is defined for values between $x=-4$ and $x=1,$ not including $x=-4$ and $x=1$ but including $x=-1.$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
x\in (-4,1)
$$

Note that the function is defined at the point $x=-1,$  even though the function jumps at that point. The function value at $x=-1$ is $2.$
